pos: n. (a district under Solomon's officer in Asher; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Aloth, probably ascents or heights, from 'alah, to go up; named once, 1 Kings 4:16.
biblical_def: Aloth occurs once, in the roll of Solomon's commissariat: “Baanah the son of Hushai was in Asher and in Aloth” (1 Kings 4:16). The office is explained at the head of the list: “And Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, which provided victuals for the king and his household: each man his month in a year made provision” (1 Kings 4:7). Twelve districts, twelve men, one month each: an arrangement of such plainness that it tells the reader more about the kingdom than any description could. The daily requirement was enormous — “And Solomon's provision for one day was thirty measures of fine flour, and threescore measures of meal” (1 Kings 4:22) — and the land bore it in a season of peace: “Judah and Israel were many, as the sand which is by the sea in multitude, eating and drinking, and making merry” (1 Kings 4:20). Where Aloth lay is not stated beyond its pairing with Asher in the north, and the dictionary leaves it there. The chapter is the high-water mark of Israel's prosperity, and a reader who knows how the book of Kings ends reads it with a certain dread, for the system that fed the court became the burden that split the kingdom under Solomon's son.

corruption_summary: Solomon's prosperity is read as the Bible's endorsement of wealth as the mark of God's favour, where Kings records the same system becoming the yoke that broke the realm.
corruption_paragraphs: A prosperity reading of 1 Kings 4 is easy to construct: peace, plenty, twelve districts bringing in provisions, and a people eating and drinking and making merry. The book itself supplies the counterweight. The same administration appears a few chapters later as forced labour and heavy taxation, and when Rehoboam refused to lighten it the ten tribes left. Scripture presents Solomon's wealth as a real gift and as a real test, and records that it was the wealth and the wives, not the enemies, that turned his heart in the end.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Lord gives both the full and the empty hand, and the full hand is the harder trial. A district named once, in a list of officers who fed a king's table for a month at a time, belongs to the brightest chapter of the monarchy and to the machinery of its division.

pos: n. (a border town of Ephraim and Benjamin; named twice, also spelt Ataroth-adar)
etymology: Hebrew 'Atroth 'Addar, crowns of Addar, from 'atarah, a crown; spelt Atarothaddar at Joshua 16:5 and Atarothadar at Joshua 18:13.
biblical_def: This town stands on the line between Ephraim and Benjamin, and the Authorized Version prints its name two ways because the Hebrew does. In Ephraim's allotment: “And the border of the children of Ephraim according to their families was thus: even the border of their inheritance on the east side was Atarothaddar, unto Bethhoron the upper” (Joshua 16:5). In Benjamin's: “And the border went over from thence toward Luz, to the side of Luz, which is Bethel, southward; and the border descended to Atarothadar, near the hill that lieth on the south side of the nether Bethhoron” (Joshua 18:13). One place, two spellings, two tribes — which is what a border town is. It is distinct from the Ataroth of Ephraim and from the Ataroth of Gad, the bare name being common enough; this one is Ataroth of Addar. The lot that set the line is described at the head of the chapter: “And the lot of the children of Joseph fell from Jordan by Jericho, unto the water of Jericho on the east, to the wilderness that goeth up from Jericho throughout mount Bethel” (Joshua 16:1), and the outcome is stated in four words of settlement: “So the children of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, took their inheritance” (Joshua 16:4).

corruption_summary: Two spellings of one town are offered as textual corruption, where the Authorized Version renders each book as it stands and the place is plainly the same.
corruption_paragraphs: Atarothaddar and Atarothadar differ by one letter, and such pairs are routinely gathered as evidence that the Hebrew text has decayed past trusting. The objection collapses on inspection: both verses place the town between Ephraim and Benjamin, near the nether Bethhoron, and no reader is in doubt which place is meant. Variation in the spelling of compound place-names is ordinary in every language with a long written history, and a translation that prints each book's form rather than silently levelling them is serving the reader, not failing him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the care Joshua's surveys take over boundaries. Chapter after chapter traces lines town by town and hill by hill, because the land was a covenant grant and not a prize, and each family's portion had to be defensible from the record. God is not careless with what He promises, down to the crowns of Addar.

pos: n. (a gate of Heshbon, named once in the Song)
etymology: Hebrew Bath-rabbim, daughter of many, from bath, a daughter, and rab, many or great; perhaps a gate facing a populous quarter; named once, Song of Solomon 7:4.
biblical_def: Bath-rabbim occurs once, in the bridegroom's praise of the bride: “Thy neck is as a tower of ivory; thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bathrabbim: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus” (Song of Solomon 7:4). The figure is of still water: deep, clear pools beside a city gate, catching the light. The name means daughter of many, which suits a gate opening on a crowded quarter, and Heshbon was a city of the Amorite king Sihon east of Jordan, taken by Israel and given to Reuben. The Song's praise runs in this register throughout: “Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners” (Song of Solomon 6:4), and “Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee” (Song of Solomon 4:7). The book is first what it says it is, a married love-song, given by inspiration to sanctify what the world cheapens; and the church has always read it also of Christ and His bride, on the warrant of the apostle's own comparison: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” (Ephesians 5:25).

corruption_summary: The Song is handled either as mere erotica or as pure allegory with no married love in it; Scripture gives it as a true song of marriage that also pictures Christ and the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors divide the Song between them. The first strips it of its typology and reads it as ancient love poetry with no more doctrine in it than any other, which leaves the church without the book the church has always used. The second strips it of its literal sense and allegorizes every image, which leaves Christian marriage without the one book of Scripture given wholly to it. The sounder course, and the Reformed one, holds both: a real bridegroom praising a real bride, and in that an image of the love of Christ for His own, on the apostle's authority (Ephesians 5:25).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not embarrassed by what He made. Marriage is one man and one woman for life, and the Holy Ghost gave the church a song in which a husband praises his wife's eyes by comparing them to pools beside a city gate. A world that has made such praise coarse has lost the thing itself.

pos: n. (a place named once as a measure of desolation, in Ezekiel's burden)
etymology: Hebrew Diblath, of uncertain location; named once, Ezekiel 6:14, in the phrase “the wilderness toward Diblath.”
biblical_def: Diblath occurs once, and is used as a yardstick for ruin: “So will I stretch out my hand upon them, and make the land desolate, yea, more desolate than the wilderness toward Diblath, in all their habitations: and they shall know that I am the LORD” (Ezekiel 6:14). Where Diblath lay Scripture does not say; it is commonly identified with Riblah on the Orontes, but that identification rests on a proposed emendation rather than on the translators' margin or on any other text, and the dictionary will not present a conjecture as knowledge. What the verse does say is plain: the land would be left emptier than the emptiest wilderness Ezekiel's hearers could name. The burden of the chapter is against the hill-shrines: “And say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD; Thus saith the Lord GOD to the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys; Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places” (Ezekiel 6:3). The slain would lie where they had worshipped: “Then shall ye know that I am the LORD, when their slain men shall be among their idols round about their altars” (Ezekiel 6:13). Yet the chapter is not without mercy, for a remnant is promised repentance: “And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives” (Ezekiel 6:9).

corruption_summary: A conjectural emendation is presented as the meaning of the text, and the judgment of the chapter is softened into natural consequence.
corruption_paragraphs: Two liberties are commonly taken here. The first is textual: because Diblath is unknown and Riblah is known, many treatments silently print Riblah and tell the reader that is what the verse says. An emendation may be worth discussing; it is not the text, and the Authorized Version is right to render what stands. The second is doctrinal: the desolation is explained as the natural result of bad politics, when the chapter has God speaking in the first person — I will stretch out my hand, I will destroy your high places — and gives the reason as idolatry, not strategy.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the purpose stated twice in the chapter: they shall know that I am the LORD. Judgment in Ezekiel is never bare destruction; it is God making Himself known where He had been denied, and the same chapter promises that those who escape will remember Him and loathe the evils they had loved.

pos: n. (a point on the northern border of Benjamin; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Geliloth, circuits or borders, from galal, to roll; named once, Joshua 18:17, over against the going up of Adummim.
biblical_def: Geliloth occurs once, in the survey of Benjamin's boundary: “And was drawn from the north, and went forth to Enshemesh, and went forth toward Geliloth, which is over against the going up of Adummim, and descended to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben” (Joshua 18:17). The name is a common noun meaning circuits or borders, pressed into service as a place-name, and the same stretch of line appears in Judah's survey from the other side: “And the border went up to Bethhogla, and passed along by the north of Betharabah; and the border went up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben” (Joshua 15:6). Benjamin's portion was the narrow strip between the two great tribes: “And the lot of the tribe of the children of Benjamin came up according to their families: and the coast of their lot came forth between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph” (Joshua 18:11), and the account closes with the settlement: “And Jordan was the border of it on the east side. This was the inheritance of the children of Benjamin, by the coasts thereof round about, according to their families” (Joshua 18:20). The going up of Adummim is the ascent from Jericho to Jerusalem — the road of the parable of the good Samaritan — so Geliloth stands beside one of the most consequential roads in Scripture.

corruption_summary: The boundary surveys are dismissed as tedious administration, where they are the legal title to a covenant promise and are written to be checked.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 15 to 19 is the part of Scripture most often skipped, and critical treatments dismiss it as priestly bookkeeping. The chapters are doing something better than that. They record the same lines twice, from the side of each neighbouring tribe, so that Judah's survey and Benjamin's meet at the stone of Bohan and agree; and they name landmarks a man could walk to. A promise written in that form is one a later generation could hold God to, which is exactly why it was written so.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's promises are particular. He did not give Israel land in general; He gave Benjamin a strip between Joseph and Judah with its corners named. The same God numbers hairs and sparrows, and the tedium of Joshua 18 is the tedium of a faithfulness that keeps its word to the yard.

pos: n. (a place in the promised enlargement of Jerusalem; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Go'ah, perhaps lowing, from ga'ah, to low as cattle; named once, Jeremiah 31:39.
biblical_def: Goath occurs once, in a promise about surveying: “And the measuring line shall yet go forth over against it upon the hill Gareb, and shall compass about to Goath” (Jeremiah 31:39). The context is the rebuilding of a city that was about to be destroyed: “Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that the city shall be built to the LORD from the tower of Hananeel unto the gate of the corner” (Jeremiah 31:38). The promise then takes in the places no one would have thought holy: “And the whole valley of the dead bodies, and of the ashes, and all the fields unto the brook of Kidron, unto the corner of the horse gate toward the east, shall be holy unto the LORD; it shall not be plucked up, nor thrown down any more for ever” (Jeremiah 31:40). The valley of dead bodies and ashes is the refuse ground, the place of burning; and it is named as part of what shall be holy. All of this stands in the same chapter as the new covenant itself: “But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jeremiah 31:33). A measuring line going out to Goath is a promise that God intends to take in the rubbish heaps.

corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 31 is pulled in two directions. Dispensational reading takes the measuring line and the horse gate as a programme of national real estate to be fulfilled apart from the church; a vague spiritualizing reading takes the new covenant and drops the city altogether. The chapter will not be split. The same paragraph that promises the law written on the heart promises that the valley of dead bodies shall be holy to the LORD, and the New Testament applies the covenant of verse 33 directly to the church in Hebrews, twice and at length.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of consecration. The line goes out past the hill, around to Goath, and takes in the ash-heaps; and the covenant it belongs to puts the law inside men rather than on tables of stone. What God rebuilds, He rebuilds to Himself, and He does not leave the refuse ground outside the wall.

pos: n. (a son of Reuben, whose stone marked the border of Judah and Benjamin; named twice)
etymology: Hebrew Bohan, a thumb, or perhaps stumpy; named twice, always in the phrase “the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben,” Joshua 15:6 and 18:17.
biblical_def: Bohan is known only by his monument. The stone that bore his name stood on the line between Judah and Benjamin, and both tribal surveys use it as a landmark. From Judah's side: “And the border went up to Bethhogla, and passed along by the north of Betharabah; and the border went up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben” (Joshua 15:6). From Benjamin's: “And was drawn from the north, and went forth to Enshemesh, and went forth toward Geliloth, which is over against the going up of Adummim, and descended to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben” (Joshua 18:17). Scripture tells us nothing else about the man: not what he did, nor when he lived, nor why a stone in the Jordan valley carried his name — only that he was of the tribe of Reuben, whose inheritance lay on the other side of the river. The surveys that use his stone are framed as covenant grants: “This then was the lot of the tribe of the children of Judah by their families” (Joshua 15:1), and “the coast of their lot came forth between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph” (Joshua 18:11). A man is remembered in the word of God for a rock with his name on it, and the rock is doing work: two tribes knew where one ended and the other began because it was there.

corruption_summary: Boundary stones are read as folk relics, where Scripture makes them legal witnesses and places a curse on moving them.
corruption_paragraphs: A named stone in a border survey invites the explanation that Israel venerated rocks, and the standard account treats such markers as the residue of an older religion of stones and pillars. The law is explicit in the other direction. Standing stones set up for worship were forbidden and ordered broken; stones set up as witnesses — Jacob's heap, Joshua's twelve out of Jordan, Bohan's stone on the line — are commended, and the law pronounces a curse on the man who removes his neighbour's landmark. The difference is between a thing worshipped and a thing testifying.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that property has a boundary and the boundary has a witness. God gave the land by lot and fixed it by landmarks, and He set His curse on quietly moving them. Honest weights, honest borders and honest records are not a lesser part of righteousness.

pos: n. (a place on the southern border of the promised land; named three times)
etymology: Hebrew 'Atsmon, bone-like or strong, from 'etsem, a bone; named three times, on the south border toward the river of Egypt.
biblical_def: Azmon marks a turn in the southern boundary of Canaan. The LORD described the line to Moses before Israel entered: “And your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim, and pass on to Zin: and the going forth thereof shall be from the south to Kadeshbarnea, and shall go on to Hazaraddar, and pass on to Azmon” (Numbers 34:4), and then, “And the border shall fetch a compass from Azmon unto the river of Egypt, and the goings out of it shall be at the sea” (Numbers 34:5). Joshua's survey repeats the line when the land was actually apportioned: “From thence it passed toward Azmon, and went out unto the river of Egypt; and the goings out of that coast were at the sea: this shall be your south coast” (Joshua 15:4). The charge that opens the description makes the nature of the gift plain: “Command the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye come into the land of Canaan; (this is the land that shall fall unto you for an inheritance, even the land of Canaan with the coasts thereof” (Numbers 34:2). The border was drawn by God and recited to a people still in the wilderness, and Azmon is one of the points on it — a name on a line that existed in the word of God before it existed on the ground.

corruption_summary: The land grant is treated as a later justification for conquest, where the border is described to Moses in the wilderness before a foot is set in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical account holds that Israel's territorial claims were written back into Moses' mouth to sanctify what the tribes later took. Numbers 34 is a poor fit for that theory in one specific respect: the border it describes is not the border Israel ever actually held. The line runs further than the tribes possessed, and the book of Joshua says frankly that much land remained unconquered. A charter forged after the fact to justify possession would describe the possession, not a larger promise the nation visibly failed to enter.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the promise is God's word before it is anyone's property. He named Azmon to a people in tents, and the naming was not conditional on their success. What Israel failed to take did not shrink the promise; it indicted the nation, which is exactly how the book of Joshua reports it.

pos: n. (the northern limit of Joshua's conquest, in the valley of Lebanon; named three times)
etymology: Hebrew Ba'al Gad, lord of fortune, from ba'al, lord or master, and gad, fortune or a troop; the northern marker of the conquered land, Joshua 11:17.
biblical_def: Baal-gad marks the far end of what Joshua took. The first notice gives the whole sweep of the campaign: “Even from the mount Halak, that goeth up to Seir, even unto Baalgad in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon: and all their kings he took, and smote them, and slew them” (Joshua 11:17). The second repeats the span in the opposite direction, in the summary of the kings defeated: “And these are the kings of the country which Joshua and the children of Israel smote on this side Jordan on the west, from Baalgad in the valley of Lebanon even unto the mount Halak, that goeth up to Seir” (Joshua 12:7). The third uses it as a boundary of land still unpossessed: “And the land of the Giblites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrising, from Baalgad under mount Hermon unto the entering into Hamath” (Joshua 13:5). The name is a heathen one, lord of fortune, which is what the Canaanites called the place; Scripture records the name without adopting the god. The conquest is summed up in a sentence that ends in rest: “So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD said unto Moses; and Joshua gave it for an inheritance unto Israel according to their divisions by their tribes. And the land rested from war” (Joshua 11:23).

corruption_summary: A heathen place-name preserved in Scripture is taken as evidence that Israel's faith was syncretistic, where the Bible records names without endorsing the gods in them.
corruption_paragraphs: Names compounded with Baal are regularly produced as proof that Israel's religion was a Canaanite variant: if the boundary marker is called lord of fortune, the argument runs, the worship must have been mixed. The inference does not follow. Scripture everywhere records the names the nations gave their places, and it does so while commanding that the names of their gods not be taken on Israelite lips; it also records that faithful kings renamed or destroyed such shrines. A map is not a creed, and reporting what a valley was called is not worship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the closing words of the chapter: the land rested from war. Joshua's conquest reached from mount Halak in the south to the lord of fortune's valley in the north, and the point of the record is not the extent but the rest — which Hebrews takes up and says was not yet the rest that remains.

pos: n. (a Canaanite royal city taken by Joshua; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Geder, a wall or hedge, from gadar, to wall up or fence; named once, Joshua 12:13, among the thirty-one kings.
biblical_def: Geder occurs once, in the list of defeated kings: “The king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one” (Joshua 12:13). The form of that chapter is the thing to notice. It is not a narrative but a tally, each king counted off with the word one, thirty-one times, ending: “The king of Tirzah, one: all the kings thirty and one” (Joshua 12:24). The chapter opens by taking in the eastern conquests too: “Now these are the kings of the land, which the children of Israel smote, and possessed their land on the other side Jordan toward the rising of the sun, from the river Arnon unto mount Hermon, and all the plain on the east” (Joshua 12:1), and the western span is given from Baal-gad to mount Halak (Joshua 12:7). The name Geder is simply the word for a wall, and the city is distinct from Gedor and from Gederah, which the dictionary treats separately. A walled town with a king of its own is reduced in the record to two words and a numeral, which is the chapter's whole argument: these were real kings in real fortresses, and they were counted like sheep.

corruption_summary: The conquest is judged by the modern law of nations and called genocide, where Scripture presents it as God's judicial act on a people long warned.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 12 is read today chiefly as an indictment of the Bible: a list of destroyed cities, celebrated. The answer is not to soften the list but to read what Scripture says about it. God told Abraham that judgment on these nations waited four centuries because their iniquity was not yet full; He warned Israel that the land would spit them out in the same way for the same sins, and it did; and He appointed the conquest as a judicial act under His own command, not as a war of national expansion. Rahab in Jericho and the Gibeonites show that the same judgment admitted whoever sought mercy.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the chapter's drumbeat: one, and one, and one, thirty-one times. Walled cities with kings over them are counted off like an inventory, because the One who gave the land is not impressed by walls. Geder means a wall, and its wall is the only thing about it the Bible records.
